query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: We hypothesize that in CoCrFeMnNi-based high-entropy alloys, doping with Al from 0 to 5 at.% modifies local short-range order (SRO), which in turn influences dislocation-mediated plastic behavior and therefore governs the retention or loss of toughness. Elevated Al content should increase SRO, restricting cross-slip and partial dislocation mobility, reducing crack-tip plasticity and diminishing toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi-based HEA, solution-annealed, with minimal short-range order before doping.
generation.intervention: Incremental Al doping (0–5 at.%) followed by standard solution annealing and quenching.
generation.conditions: Fracture toughness tests performed in air at ambient and sub-ambient temperatures to isolate the effect of SRO.
generation.structural_mediator: Locally increased short-range chemical order in the doped alloys.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced short-range order decreases dislocation mobility, restricting dislocation slip and cross-slip, thereby reducing plasticity at the crack tip and decreasing toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: As Al content increases, the fracture toughness will systematically decrease in correlation with SRO development, particularly at lower temperatures where dislocation-mediated plasticity is prominent.
generation.baseline: Undoped CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy with minimal SRO and higher fracture toughness.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds for CoCrFeMnNi-based HEAs doped with low to moderate Al content (0–5 at.%) under conventional solution-annealing conditions. Excessively high Al content or distinct ternary additions might change the dominant strengthening/toughening mechanisms, invalidating the hypothesis.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative effects of Al doping on SRO are not fully established, and alternative nanoscale features (e.g., precipitates) may also influence toughness in certain compositions or processing routes.

falsification_experiment.design: Process multiple CoCrFeMnNi-based HEA ingots with varying Al contents (0, 1, 3, and 5 at.%), subject them to the same solution annealing and quenching procedure, and evaluate their fracture toughness using standardized (e.g., ASTM E399) testing. Perform localized compositional and structural analyses (e.g., APT, XRD, TEM) to characterize the extent of SRO or precipitate formation.
measurements: Atom probe tomography of doped and undoped samples to map local chemical order (SRO) and identify any precipitates.
Fracture toughness KIC values at ambient and sub-ambient temperatures.
In situ or ex situ TEM imaging of crack-tip region to identify dominant plastic deformation and crack-bridging mechanisms.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis would be falsified if the increase in Al content does not alter the extent of short-range order or the presence of shear-fault binding, and if the fracture toughness remains the same or increases even as Al doping is increased.

cited_evidence.text: We believe that the excellent strength, ductility and toughness of this high-entropy alloy results directly from this synergy of intrinsic (plasticity related) and extrinsic (shielding related) mechanisms, which (unlike traditional toughening mechanisms involving mainly precipitates and/or boundaries) primarily result from its special material characteristics of a low average SFE with possible variation of local SFE (that modulates the behaviour of full and partial dislocations locally), and high lattice friction (that provides strengthening from the increased resistance to the planar slip of dislocations and its influence on the motion of partial dislocations), the low SFE further contributing to the remarkable formation of nanoscale crack bridges within a few hundred nanometres of the crack tip. (Further deliberations on the controlling factors for this synergy of deformation mechanisms are described in Supplementary Note 3). Recently, Ding et al. synthesized FCC CoCrFeNiPd and CoCrFeNiMn HEAs. The former exhibited a higher yield strength than the latter with comparable tensile ductility. They proposed that the essential difference between these two HEAs was associated with atomic segregation and short-range ordering (SRO); both were enhanced in CoCrFeNiPd, as compared with CoCrFeNiMn. The idea was that SRO tends to create resistance to deformation/slip, leading to larger dislocation glide resistance in the more ordered CoCrFeNiPd than in CoCrFeNiMn HEAs. Theoretical work by Yin et al. suggested that the strengthening was due mainly to the large atomic/misfit volume of Pd in CoCrFeNi. Ma et al. identified a number of unusual features associated with dislocations/slips in HEAs that were related to lattice distortion and/or local chemical order. SRO also occurs in medium-entropy alloys (MEAs). The atomic structure of a CoCrNi MEA indicates that Cr favors Ni and Co neighbors, reducing the electrical and thermal conductivities and increasing the stacking-fault energies and hardness.

Hybrid MC/MD simulations have proven to be a powerful tool to explore the effects of atomic segregation and SRO on the mechanical properties of MEAs and HEAs. For example, Jian et al. used hybrid MC and MD simulations to investigate the role of lattice distortion (LD) and SRO on the formation and evolution of dislocations in a CoCrNi MEA. These simulations suggested that yield strength was controlled by the strain required to nucleate Shockley partial dislocations; LD lowered this strain, while SRO increased it. The hybrid MC/MD simulations of Li et al. demonstrated that increasing SRO in the CoCrNi MEA increased the ruggedness of the energy landscape, thereby raising barriers to dislocation activity and increasing strength. Short-range ordering in HEAs is more complex than that of MEAs (with the increased number of distinct atomic pairs in HEAs), suggesting that HEAs provide a richer environment for tailoring their orders and microstructures to achieve superior strength and ductility. Is it possible to introduce SRO in HEAs to enhance both strength and ductility? If so, what microstructures are required? And, what is the underlying mechanistic reason for these increases? The exceptional mechanical strength of medium/high-entropy alloys has been attributed to hardening in random solid solutions. Here, we evidence non-random chemical mixing in a CrCoNi alloy, resulting from short-range ordering. A data-mining approach of electron nanodiffraction enabled the study, which is assisted by neutron scattering, atom probe tomography, and diffraction simulation using first-principles theory models. Two samples, one homogenized and one heat-treated, are observed. In both samples, results reveal two types of short-range-order inside nanoclusters that minimize the Cr–Cr nearest neighbors (L12) or segregate Cr on alternating close-packed planes (L11). The L11 is predominant in the homogenized sample, while the L12 formation is promoted by heat-treatment, with the latter being accompanied by a dramatic change in dislocation-slip behavior. These findings uncover short-range order and the resulted chemical heterogeneities behind the mechanical strength in CrCoNi, providing general opportunities for atomistic-structure study in concentrated alloys for the design of strong and ductile materials. occupying_moves.lever: Systematic variation of specific elemental additions (e.g., Al) to tune short-range order
occupying_moves.technique: Mechanical (fracture toughness) testing combined with microstructural analyses (TEM, XRD, SEM-EBSD)
occupying_moves.conditions: Vary Al content from 0–5 at.% in a base high-entropy alloy, perform solution annealing and subsequent quenching, then test at multiple temperatures to track toughness changes

chosen.lever: Al doping to modify local short-range order
chosen.technique: Controlled composition design, fracture toughness tests (ASTM E399) and detailed microstructural characterization
chosen.conditions: Alloys with stepwise increments of Al content, identical processing routes, ambient and sub-ambient temperature testing
chosen.why: Compositional variation is a direct and standard approach for revealing how short-range order and associated dislocation mechanisms govern toughness in HEAs. Measuring toughness across a series of Al-doped compositions provides a clear test of the hypothesis that localized chemical ordering controls ductility and crack resistance.
